full_text:
PSA: You can't both ridicule the idea of raspberry pi validators AND advocate for 1 ETH validators

If we want 1 ETH validators, we need to lower the cost of the hardware that validators are run on. The cheapest you can run hardware at home right now is ~$800. A @dappnode costs minimum $1500

With a 32 ETH bond, it takes ~3-7 months to make up the (minimum) cost of that hardware. With a 1 ETH bond, it would take ~10-18 years to make up the cost of that hardware. Hardware needs to be replaced after 3-4 years

I'm an advocate of hardware requirements staying where they are for now, but I can't reasonably also advocate for 1 ETH validators at the same time

1 ETH validators would be amazing, but we need to prioritize one or the other and it seems the community has chosen scaling over smaller form factor validators, so I'm going with that

imo, the timeline for hardware cost recoup needs to be kept under 1 year for it to be economically feasible for someone to decide to run a validator from home

Economies of scale are difficult but not unbeatable, we shouldn’t just steer into them. 

If Ethereum had a 1/n honesty assumption, that might work, but I don’t think there are >50% of stakeweight ideologues though :( 

I get the hope on too much hassle route, but I don’t think you sufficiently account for the fact that the etf providers make money on fees, not on real rates. The ideologues will have similar labour and hardware costs, but only a fraction of the billions of dollars of tvl the ETFs will have.

Strong agree there. Maybe where our assumptions differ is on how high issuance can recover to with a cap in place. I highly doubt it ever goes above 0.5% again, because that’s plenty to make profit with a billion/10 billion TVL. I’ve seen others that assume equilibrium is at 2% but I think there is ~zero chance of that without liveness penalties or other new risks being introduced.

And at 0.5%, ~$100k for a validator, a very optimistically low cost of $100 p/a to solo stake on something slightly above a raspberry pi, you pay 20% ‘fees’, versus the ~10% you’d pay to delegate. Which borders on altruism/ideology/sunk cost accounting territory in my book.
